text:
**Recommendation:** Run a six-week teen "maker studio" rather than a reading programme. Teens build something they care about (a zine, a short audio or video piece, a game, or a podcast episode) in a weekly two-hour drop-in session, with the library's collection and staff serving the project rather than being the topic. The programme is called something that does not contain the words "book" or "reading". Participants finish with a public showcase in week six. Measurement centres on a short before-and-after survey, a behaviour count (library cards and items borrowed), and a work sample, all collected inside the six weeks.

**Librarian time (4 hours a week).** Two hours is the session itself. One hour goes to preparation and volunteer briefing. One hour goes to recruitment in weeks 0 to 2 and, afterwards, to data collection and showcase planning. Two recruited volunteers, such as local college students, a community artist, or a teen-services volunteer, co-run each session so the librarian is not the sole adult. Before week one, spend about three hours of non-programme time, ideally borrowed from outreach duties, on recruitment; if that is impossible, recruit during weeks minus two to zero using the hour allocation above.

**Weekly structure and why teens would come.** The hook is autonomy, a social setting, and a tangible product, not literature. Each session runs two hours with free food, a loose start, and no sign-up beyond week one.

Week 1: Pick a project. Teens choose a format (zine, podcast, short film, comic, game design) in small groups, make a team name, and take a short interest survey. Week 2: Skills session. A volunteer teaches the basics of their format, such as layout, recording, or storyboarding. Week 3: Research and raw material. This is where the collection quietly enters. Teams pull reference images, true-crime or sports material, graphic novels, music histories, or manga for their project, and the librarian helps them find sources. They check out items as inspiration, and borrowing happens because it is useful, not required. Week 4: Make. A full work session with volunteer support. Week 5: Polish and rehearse. Teams give each other feedback and prepare for the showcase. Week 6: Showcase. Families and friends are invited, work is displayed or played, and teams receive certificates. Completed pieces are offered to the library's teen collection or website with consent.

Why this works for non-readers: it is a social space with food, the entry task requires no reading, they own the topic, and the end product gives them something to show others. Attendance risk is highest in weeks 3 and 4, so each week ends with a clear next step and a text reminder to those who opted in.

**Recruitment of non-users.** Do not rely on library signage. Spend librarian hours in weeks minus two to zero on the places teens already are. Contact the local middle and high school counsellors, art, media, and English teachers to run a five-minute pitch and a sign-up sheet. Approach youth sports clubs, skate parks, after-school programmes, and local youth services. Ask volunteers and any known teen staff to share via their networks. Use a simple one-page flyer and a short social post designed by a teen volunteer rather than the library's usual look. Offer a trial: bring a friend, and the first session needs no registration. Aim for 15 registered teens, expecting 8 to 12 regular attendees. Record at sign-up whether each teen has a library card and whether they visited in the previous three months, so you can show how many were genuinely new users.

**Budget ($500).** Food and drink at six sessions, about $20 per session for 12 teens: $120. Materials such as paper, printing for zines and the showcase, markers, and a pack of cheap audio and art supplies: $110. Two USB microphones or a shared audio kit, plus a basic tripod: $90. Volunteer thank-you and training, such as gift cards and a short briefing: $50. Recruitment printing and a small social ad or sign-up incentive: $40. Showcase food, certificates, and framing: $50. Contingency: $40. This leaves nothing for stipends or equipment beyond the basics, so use free software (Audacity, Canva, Twine, free video editors) and the library's existing computers.

**Measuring outcomes beyond attendance.** Collect four things, each cheap and doable within six weeks.

First, a one-page pre-and-post survey (week 1 and week 6, five minutes, on paper) with 4 to 5 questions on a five-point scale: I feel the library is a place for people like me; I know how to find information I need; I feel confident finishing a creative project; I would come to the library again on my own; and one open question, "What is one thing the library could offer you?" The shift in mean scores is the main outcome.

Second, behaviour data from the library system: new cards issued to participants, items borrowed during and in the four weeks after the programme if timing allows, and independent visits (staff note when a participant is seen outside session times). Compare with the baseline of zero or low use recorded at sign-up.

Third, a completion measure: the share of registered teens who finish and present a piece. This tests whether the programme changed what they did, not only whether they attended.

Fourth, a short exit interview or voice note with six to eight participants in week 6, and one comment card from parents at the showcase.

**Caveats.** With 10 to 15 teens, results show direction, not proof; there is no control group, and self-reported confidence may be inflated. State a repeat threshold in advance, for example: at least half of regular attendees complete a project, mean "library is for me" scores rise by at least one point, and at least a third of new teens get a card or borrow an item. Open questions: whether school contacts will respond in time, whether two reliable volunteers can be found, and whether the chosen formats suit the local teens, which the week 1 survey should confirm before materials are bought.
